text:
This is Moth and Gravel, Field
Notes. Today, a question that

connects three studies. What
does an interface let you

believe? This is an AI generated
conversation adapted from the

published notes. The source
studies concern software

contracts, a little robot's map,
and a telemetry dashboard. All

three give a person a quick
picture. A green light, a

colored map, a number that sits
quietly on a gauge. The picture

can feel more certain than the
information behind it. Let's

start with the green light. It
is a very efficient piece of

design. One glance, one small
exhale. The thing is all right.

What thing? And all right in
what sense? A service can be

running, a test can pass, a
result can be delivered. Those

answer different questions, even
when the interface gives them

the same color. Field Note 5
follows that distinction across

three projects. In Gayanu, which
is being developed as a

workspace companion, a healthy
runtime is an observation about

the runtime. Whether a feature
meets its acceptance conditions

needs its own evidence. The
source contract also keeps a

failed runtime probe unknown. If
the observation did not succeed,

it has not established that the
application stopped. That sounds

like a small wording distinction
until someone acts on the wrong

version. It becomes even more
interesting in Ajo, which checks

agent plans and records their
execution. The note describes a

local integration report in
which all 34 acceptance cases

passed. The delivery records
still included incomplete,

unknown, and unresolved
outcomes. That is possible

because some cases are meant to
preserve those outcomes. If a

case asks the mechanism to
refuse an unsafe next step, a

correct refusal is a pass. If
the acknowledgement was lost,

keeping that outcome unknown can
also be correct. The report

records six verified delivery
sub-probes separately from the

passing cases. A concise
headline needs a route back to

that distinction. And those
fixtures are not a sample for

calculating a general delivery
success rate. The note is

reading bounded results. It does
not establish production

reliability or release
readiness. Paja, a build tool

for spare machines, gives green
a more modest job. Every

configured step exited with
zero. It's recorded result

distinguishes failed steps,
infrastructure failures,

cancellation, and timeouts. That
boundary can be understood.

Inspect the recipe, then ask
whether the configured steps

establish what you care about.
The indicator has a clear job.

It does not have to quietly
promise every possible property

of the software. So, the useful
design question is, what can

this green light honestly let's
one stop worrying about? And

what still deserves a question
of its own? The same problem

turns up in Field Note 6 about
the Kitronic Buggy. A little

robot has an ultrasonic sensor,
motors, and tools for giving its

readings a visual form. A few
colored points begin to look

like a room. A drawing is
persuasive. A blank region can

look like empty floor even when
the machine is not established

that the space is free. The
current firmware begins its

occupancy grid at a neutral
prior. As observations arrive,

parts of the sensor beam receive
free space updates and the

endpoint receives occupied space
updates. Confidence affects the

contribution and later
observations can strengthen or

revise the picture. There are
three answers to preserve. Free,

occupied, and undecided. The
stored value thresholds are not

probabilities. Values below 80
are classified as free. Values

above 170 are occupied. Values
from 80 through 170 remain

unclassified. The initial value
is 128. In the camera overlay,

unclassified cells remain
unpainted. That leaves the

unanswered question visible. The
saved scan viewer also offers

several views of the same input.
A polar plot, a top-down view,

an occupancy grid, and a
distance profile. One view can

question the attractive one, but
the person needs to know which

frame the marks belong to and
whether they came from a current

observation or a saved example.
Position is part of the estimate

too. The grid belongs to a world
frame while the robot's

estimated position changes
inside it. The source uses motor

time kinematics with selective
heading correction. A calibrated

camera marker supplies another
position estimate. Showing two

trails together can make a
disagreement visible. It does

not establish that either trail
is accurate. This note reads

mapping source and an offline
replay of saved sample data. It

does not establish calibrated
map accuracy, safe navigation,

or full simultaneous
localization and mapping. No

live hardware or camera session
was run for the note. The

proposed reader study is still
ahead. Ask someone which parts

the robot has not established.
Ask which position they believe

and why. Watch what they infer
from a blank area. That is a

concrete way to ask whether
uncertainty survived the

drawing. It is also a question
about attention, which brings us

to Field Note 7. Fast signals,
slow eyes. The telemetry

dashboard keeps the latest
received readings in shared

state. The interface draws its
gauges from that state, then

schedules its next update 33
milliseconds later. That is a

requested pause after drawing,
not a measured frame rate. The

drawing takes time. Other work
in the window takes time.

Calling it 30 frames per second
would claim something the source

reading is not measured. A quiet
number creates another question.

It can stay on screen after the
machine has stopped sending

packets. Without a condition
beside it, the last answer can

look like the present answer. At
a refresh, the dashboard checks

the age of the latest packet.
Less than half a second gets the

label connected. At half a
second or more, the label

becomes stale data. The gauges
still show the latest received

values. So, the number remains
available, but its relationship

to now has changed. And the
label changes when the next

interface update checks the age
rather than at a separately

established instant. A stale
packet does not establish the

robot's physical state. The
design needs to help someone

notice the gap without turning
every arrival into a demand for

attention. The latest packet
gauges do not retain every

intermediate value. Packet
counters and a recent arrival

rate view provided different
kind of evidence about the

stream. A calm display and a
detailed record serve different

kinds of attention. That is the
shared thread. Each picture

needs a clear account of what it
knows. A green light needs a

scope. A map needs room for
undecided space. A current value

needs a condition about
freshness. And each study has a

practical next question. Can a
person tell running from

delivered? Can they find the
space the robot has not

established? Can they notice
when a reading has become old?

Those are proposed questions,
not completed comprehension

studies. Their answers will
matter more than how reassuring

the pictures feel to their
makers. You have been listening

to Moth and Gravel, Field Notes.
What does the interface let you

believe? The written sources are
notes 5, 6, and 7 at

mothandgravel.com. They keep the
detailed boundaries,

illustrations, and study scope
available to inspect. A useful

interface gives someone a place
to look and a reason to trust

what that place actually
establishes.
